q: During the year an individual had short-term capital gains of $5,000, short-term capital losses of $8,000, long-term capital gains of $10,000 and long-term capital losses of $4,000. What is the net result of these transactions?
exp: Short-term items net to a $3,000 loss and long-term items to a $6,000 gain; offsetting gives a $3,000 net long-term capital gain eligible for preferential rates. Stopping after the long-term netting gives $6,000.

q: Hana, an individual, had a $2,000 short-term capital loss and a $6,000 long-term capital loss this year and no capital gains. What is her capital loss deduction and carryover?
exp: Individuals deduct up to $3,000 of net capital loss, using short-term losses first ($2,000) and then $1,000 of long-term loss, so the $5,000 carryover is long-term and has no expiration. Using the long-term loss first gives the mixed carryover.

q: A C corporation has $100,000 of ordinary taxable income and a $20,000 net capital loss for the current year. It had net capital gains in each of the three prior years. How is the capital loss treated?
choices: Deduct $3,000 against ordinary income and carry $17,000 forward indefinitely
Deduct the full $20,000 against ordinary income
Deduct nothing currently; carry the $20,000 back three years and forward five years as a short-term capital loss
Deduct nothing currently; carry the $20,000 forward indefinitely as a long-term capital loss
exp: Corporations may use capital losses only against capital gains; a net capital loss is carried back three years and forward five years, always as a short-term loss. The $3,000 allowance and indefinite carryforward apply only to individuals.

q: Ivy sold business equipment she had held for four years for $70,000. It cost $100,000 and she had claimed $60,000 of depreciation. What is the amount and character of her gain?
exp: Gain is $70,000 - $40,000 basis = $30,000, and §1245 recaptures as ordinary income the lesser of the gain or depreciation taken ($60,000), so all $30,000 is ordinary. §1231 treatment applies only to gain above total depreciation.

q: Jake sold business machinery held for five years for $115,000. It cost $100,000, and he had claimed $60,000 of depreciation. What is the character of his gain?
exp: Total gain is $115,000 - $40,000 = $75,000; §1245 recaptures depreciation of $60,000 as ordinary income, and the $15,000 excess over original cost is §1231 gain. Treating the whole gain as ordinary ignores the cap at depreciation taken.

q: Kai, an individual, sold an office building held for ten years for $600,000. It cost $500,000 and he had claimed $150,000 of straight-line depreciation. Ignore land. How is the $250,000 gain treated?
choices: $150,000 unrecaptured §1250 gain taxed at a maximum 25% rate and $100,000 §1231 gain
$250,000 §1231 gain taxed entirely at the regular long-term capital gain rates
exp: §1250 recaptures only depreciation in excess of straight line, so there is no ordinary recapture, but the $150,000 of straight-line depreciation is unrecaptured §1250 gain taxed at up to 25%. Treating the depreciation as ordinary income applies the §1245 rule to real property.

q: Delta Corp., a C corporation, recognized a $300,000 gain when it disposed of a warehouse used in its business for eight years. Delta had paid $800,000 for the warehouse (ignore land), deducted $200,000 of straight-line depreciation, and received $900,000. How much of the gain is ordinary income?
exp: §291 makes a corporation treat 20% of the lesser of straight-line depreciation or gain as ordinary income: 20% x $200,000 = $40,000; the remaining $260,000 is §1231 gain. Taking 20% of the total gain gives $60,000.

q: An individual with no §1231 losses in prior years had $20,000 of §1231 gains and $25,000 of §1231 losses this year, with no recapture. How is the net amount treated?
choices: $3,000 ordinary loss and $2,000 capital loss carryover
exp: A net §1231 loss is an ordinary loss, fully deductible without the $3,000 capital loss limit. Treating it as a capital loss applies the rule for net §1231 gains in reverse.

q: This year an individual has a net §1231 gain of $30,000. Over the prior five years she had $12,000 of net §1231 losses that have not been recaptured. How is the current $30,000 net §1231 gain treated?
choices: $12,000 ordinary income and $18,000 long-term capital gain
$18,000 ordinary income and $12,000 long-term capital gain
exp: Under the five-year lookback rule, net §1231 gain is ordinary to the extent of unrecaptured net §1231 losses of the prior five years ($12,000); the remaining $18,000 is long-term capital gain. Ignoring the lookback gives $30,000 of capital gain.

q: Lia sold business equipment she had used for eight months, recognizing a $3,000 loss. How is the loss treated?
choices: No deduction until the equipment is fully depreciated
exp: Depreciable business property is excluded from capital assets, and it is §1231 property only if held more than one year, so a loss on equipment held eight months is an ordinary loss. Calling it a short-term capital loss treats business equipment as a capital asset.

q: Which of the following is a capital asset in the hands of the taxpayer?
choices: Inventory held for sale to customers
Accounts receivable from sales of inventory
A copyright on a novel written by the taxpayer
exp: Property held for personal use, such as a residence, is a capital asset under §1221. Inventory, receivables from its sale, and a copyright held by the author who created it are specifically excluded.

q: Mo and Nan file jointly. They bought original-issue stock directly from a small corporation that qualifies under §1244, and this year the stock became worthless, producing a $130,000 loss. How is the loss treated?
exp: §1244 allows an ordinary loss of up to $100,000 per year on a joint return ($50,000 otherwise); the $30,000 excess is a capital loss. The $50,000 limit applies to single filers.

q: In 2016, Ola bought at original issue $1,000,000 of stock in a domestic C corporation that met all the qualified small business stock requirements. This year she sold the stock for $6,000,000. What amount of the gain is included in her gross income?
exp: For qualified small business stock acquired after September 27, 2010 and held more than five years, §1202 excludes 100% of the gain up to the greater of $10 million or 10 times basis, so the $5,000,000 gain is fully excluded. The 50% exclusion applies only to much older stock.

q: Pia has a $10,000 long-term gain on collectibles, a $5,000 long-term gain on stock and a $4,000 net short-term capital loss. How are her net gains grouped for rate purposes?
exp: A net short-term capital loss first offsets gain in the highest-rate (28%) group, leaving $6,000 of collectibles gain and $5,000 of 15% gain. Offsetting the stock gain first increases the amount taxed at 28%.

q: Quinn sold business equipment that cost $50,000, on which $30,000 of depreciation had been taken, for $60,000. He received $12,000 in the year of sale and a note for the balance payable in later years. He did not elect out of the installment method. How much gain does Quinn recognize in the year of sale?
exp: §1245 recapture ($30,000) is recognized in full in the year of sale; the remaining $10,000 gain is reported under the installment method at a gross profit ratio of $10,000 / $60,000, so $12,000 x 1/6 = $2,000, for a total of $32,000. Applying the installment method to the entire gain gives $8,000.

q: Rex died owning business equipment that cost $100,000, had $70,000 of depreciation, and was worth $60,000 at his death. His son inherited the equipment. What is the son's basis, and what happens to the depreciation recapture potential?
choices: Basis $60,000; the $30,000 recapture potential is eliminated
Basis $30,000; the recapture potential carries over to the son
Basis $60,000; $30,000 of ordinary income is reported on Rex's final return
Basis $30,000; the son reports $30,000 of ordinary income
exp: Transfers at death are an exception to §1245 recapture, and the heir takes a stepped-up basis equal to fair market value, so the recapture potential disappears. By contrast, a gift carries over basis and recapture potential to the donee.

q: Sal, whose AGI is large, donated business equipment held three years to a qualified public charity. The equipment cost $40,000, had $30,000 of depreciation, and was worth $30,000. What is Sal's charitable contribution deduction?
exp: The deduction is reduced by the amount that would be ordinary income if the property were sold: §1245 recapture of $20,000 (the lesser of gain or depreciation), so $30,000 - $20,000 = $10,000. Deducting full fair market value ignores the recapture reduction.

q: Tom purchased a business that included a customer list (a §197 intangible) for $150,000. After claiming $40,000 of amortization, he sold the customer list for $160,000. How is the gain treated?
exp: Amortizable §197 intangibles are treated as §1245 property, so amortization taken ($40,000) is recaptured as ordinary income and the $10,000 excess over cost is §1231 gain. Treating the whole gain as §1231 ignores recapture of amortization.

q: Una wrote a call option on stock she owns and received a $2,000 premium. The option expired unexercised 14 months later. How does Una treat the premium?
choices: A $2,000 reduction in the basis of her stock
exp: Under §1234, the writer of an option that lapses has a short-term capital gain regardless of how long the option was outstanding. A basis reduction would apply only to a purchaser who exercises a put, not to a lapsed written call.

q: Vic, an individual inventor, transferred all substantial rights to a patent he developed to an unrelated manufacturer in exchange for royalties based on production, three months after the patent was issued. How is Vic's income treated?
choices: Ordinary income, because the patent was held less than one year
Long-term capital gain, regardless of how long the patent was held
exp: §1235 treats a transfer of all substantial rights to a patent by its individual holder as a sale of a long-term capital asset, even if payments are contingent on production and the holding period is short. Treating it as short-term ignores this special rule.

q: Wes owns 100% of the stock of W Corp. He sold W Corp a building he had used in his business for $250,000; its cost was $200,000 and he had claimed $40,000 of straight-line depreciation. W Corp will depreciate the building. How is Wes's $90,000 gain treated?
exp: §1239 treats all gain on a sale of depreciable property to a controlled entity (more than 50% owned) as ordinary income, overriding §1231 and the 25% rate. The split answer applies only to sales to unrelated buyers.

q: An individual with no prior §1231 losses had a $10,000 net §1231 gain, a $2,000 long-term capital gain and a $4,000 short-term capital loss. What is the individual's net capital gain?
exp: The net §1231 gain is treated as long-term capital gain, so long-term gains total $12,000; netting against the $4,000 short-term loss leaves an $8,000 net capital gain. Leaving the §1231 gain out of the capital netting gives the wrong total.

q: An individual had the following, all on business property held more than one year: a $8,000 casualty gain on a building (no depreciation recapture), a $3,000 casualty loss on equipment, and a $7,000 loss on the sale of business land. How are these items treated?
exp: Casualty items are netted first; the $5,000 net casualty gain enters the main §1231 netting with the $7,000 land loss, producing a $2,000 net §1231 loss, which is ordinary. Treating the net loss as capital ignores §1231's favorable loss rule.

q: A C corporation has $100,000 of ordinary taxable income and a $50,000 net long-term capital gain. Assume the corporate rate is 21%. What is its regular income tax?
exp: Corporations have no preferential capital gain rate, so all $150,000 is taxed at 21% = $31,500. Applying a 15% rate to the gain gives $28,500, which is the individual rate structure.

q: A real estate developer subdivided a tract of land and sold lots to home buyers in the ordinary course of business. The lots had been held for three years. How is the developer's gain treated?
exp: Property held primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of business is excluded from both capital asset and §1231 treatment, so the gain is ordinary regardless of holding period. The three-year holding period is irrelevant for a dealer.

q: Which of the following is §1231 property?
choices: Equipment used in the business for six months
Land held as an investment for five years
Land used as a business parking lot for three years
exp: §1231 property is depreciable or real property used in a trade or business and held more than one year, which includes business land. Investment land is a capital asset, and equipment held six months fails the holding period.

q: Yan bought equipment for $40,000 and expensed the entire cost under §179. Two years later she sold it for $25,000. How is the sale treated?
exp: §179 expense is treated as depreciation for recapture, so the basis is $0 and the $25,000 gain is recaptured as ordinary income under §1245 (lesser of gain or $40,000 deducted). Treating the gain as §1231 ignores the expensing.

q: Zoe, an individual, has a $50,000 long-term capital loss carryover from prior years. This year her only capital transaction is a $10,000 long-term capital gain. What is her capital loss carryover to next year?
exp: The carryover offsets the $10,000 gain, leaving a $40,000 net loss, of which $3,000 is deducted against ordinary income and $37,000 carries forward indefinitely. Forgetting the $3,000 deduction gives $40,000; individuals' carryovers do not expire after five years.

q: Abe, an individual whose long-term capital gain rate is 20%, sold a rental building and recognized a $100,000 gain, of which $40,000 is unrecaptured §1250 gain; the rest is §1231 gain treated as long-term capital gain. Assume the maximum rate on unrecaptured §1250 gain is 25% and his ordinary rate is 35%. Ignoring the net investment income tax, what is the tax on the gain?
exp: The unrecaptured §1250 gain is taxed at 25% ($10,000) and the remaining $60,000 at 20% ($12,000), for $22,000. Taxing all $100,000 at 20% gives $20,000.

q: Bo, a single investor, bought 1,000 shares of a corporation's stock from its founder for $40,000. The stock met all §1244 requirements when the corporation issued it to the founder. This year the stock became worthless. How does Bo treat the loss?
choices: $40,000 ordinary loss deductible over five years
exp: §1244 ordinary loss treatment is available only to the individual (or partnership) to whom the corporation originally issued the stock, so a purchaser from the founder has a capital loss. Assuming §1244 status follows the shares is the trap.
